newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Thyssen-Krupp steel titan rattles Germany.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thyssen-Krupp steel titan rattles Germany.

text.p: German steel workers maintained their mass protests in the country's industrial heartland on Thursday after Thyssen and Krupp sealed a merger that will create a new steel giant but cost 8,000 jobs.
Thousands of angry workers at three Krupp Hoesch steel mills went on strike in an attempt to secure written confirmation of management pledges that none of them would face compulsory redundancy.

Their fears reflect the way the deal to merge the quality steel production of Thyssen and Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp has shaken Germany's tradition of cooperation between industry, workers, banks and government.

The new joint venture merger, which began as a bank-financed hostile takeover bid by Krupp, will create a behemoth that can spew out 15 million tonnes of steel a year, equal in might to France's Usinor-Sacilor or British Steel.

Two other areas where Thyssen and Krupp Hoesch already cooperate will not be part of the deal: Krupp Thyssen Nirosta, the world's biggest stainless steel maker, which is controlled by Krupp, and a Thyssen-led tinplate venture.

The new company, Thyssen Krupp Stahl AG, will concentrate hot metal operations at Thyssen's main Duisburg steel works, shutting down three blast furnaces at Krupp's Dortmund plant, and expand rolling and processing activities at Krupp Hoesch.

Thyssen will hold 60 percent of the new company and Krupp Hoesch will hold a 40 percent share. The deal could achieve annual savings of 550 million marks ($325 million), analysts say, to help finance the job cuts and trim the combined workforce to 18,000.
The companies have promised there will be no compulsory redundancies, but economists, like the striking workers, also questioned whether Thyssen and Krupp would be able to keep their word.
"This promise is an uncovered cheque for the future," said Heinz Schrumpf of the Rheinisch Westfaelisches economic institute, which specialises in the steel industry.
"I have my doubts that compulsory layoffs can be ruled out as easily as the workers think."

The new job cuts are just the latest in a wave of consolidation that began with West Germany's first postwar steel crisis in 1975. The industry then began a bloodletting that slashed the workforce of nearly 350,000 to 110,000 by 1995 at the end of the most recent steel slump.

Restructuring in the former East Germany has been just as severe. There were 80,000 steel workers in the east at the end of 1989, just before German unification in 1990, compared to around 10,000 today.
And cuts in jobs and production in the steel sector, unforeseen just two weeks ago, will have a broad impact on coal mining as the steel industry's demand for coke falls with output cuts.
This could force coal miners, who pushed Chancellor Helmut Kohl into cushioning the effect of swingeing subsidy cuts with mass protests two weeks ago, to demand that Bonn reopen that issue.

Unemployment in the Ruhr, Germany's "rust belt", already stands at 15.3 percent, three points above the national average, at a time when the number of unemployed has reached a level not seen since 1933.
But any increase in aid to Germany's smokestack industries is unwelcome as Bonn seeks to cut spending and avert the threat of failing to qualify for Europe's single currency.
The merger has also claimed other victims.
Deutsche Bank board member Ulrich Cartellieri was widely expected to give up his seat on Thyssen's supervisory board on Thursday.
Cartellieri sits on Thyssen's supervisory board but failed to mention that his bank was leading the consortium prepared to provide a 15 billion mark facility to Krupp to support its hostile bid.
($ = 1.681 German Marks)
